content.thinking:
I don't think I need a specific kit for this whimsical style, so I'll handle eye decals with plain SVG myself. I'm sketching proportions for the capybara—real-world size is roughly 1-1.3m long, 0.5m tall, 50kg—then thinking about how to exaggerate those for a whimsical take.

I'm picturing a chunky barrel-bodied capybara with a blocky, oversized snout, tiny ears, and small high-set eyes, topped with a cheerful round bird (blue and yellow, chick-like) perched on its head, complete with its own mini-skeleton for wings, tail, and beak. I'm working out the full skeleton for the capybara too—root hips, spine chain, stubby webbed legs, a small tail stub, and separate upper/lower jaw joints for the blunt, boxy snout, placing the nostrils on top of the muzzle.

Now I'm mapping out the body's loft stations along the spine in meters—rump, hips, mid, shoulders, and neck base—each with width and height values to build the rounded barrel shape, then figuring out belly clearance for the short legs and starting to plan the head's position and joint placement.

Continuing the head loft: skull, mid-head, and muzzle stations with their own widths and heights, giving a tall blocky capybara snout rather than a pointed one, with the head sized large relative to the body for a whimsical look. I'm noting capybaras barely have a neck, so I'm starting to sketch the spine chain from hips through chest into the head area.

Still defining joint chains...

Actually simpler: hips as root aimed forward, spine path starting a bit further forward around z=-0.2. The body loft uses bones hips, spine, neck with the path segmented by joint projection, so the rump section behind hips still belongs to the hips bone. For the head I'll build the upper skull as a loft skinned to the head joint, with the jaw as a separate joint positioned below for independent movement.

Now I'm working out where the mouth line sits so the lower jaw tucks under the snout properly, setting station widths and heights front to back so the upper head profile narrows toward the nose and widens at the skull while leaving room below for the jaw box.

Adding the mouth line with a tiny dark decal, plus two whimsical buck teeth poking from the upper lip near the front. I'm also placing a blunt, rounded nose pad at the top-front with small dark nostril ellipsoids for that classic capybara look.

Now positioning the eyes high on the sides of the head, giving them big shiny dark spheres with a tiny highlight and eyelid decal for a cute, exaggerated expression.

For the ears, I'll place small rounded pinkish-brown shapes toward the top-back of the head with darker inner cavities, tilting them slightly outward for a whimsical look.

For the legs, I'm working out joint placement so the shoulder-to-foot chain spans the right distance with a slight bend, using a two-segment limb with shoulder, elbow, and wrist joints — treating front legs with the same "leg" role as the back for simplicity in a quadruped structure.

For toes, I'm balancing detail against joint budget: four front toes and three hind toes per foot would mean 28 joints if fully rigged, which stays under the 160 limit, but simplifying to single-joint chains per toe (14 joints total) using a sprout loop keeps things lighter while still giving each digit independent movement.

For the feet shape, I'm envisioning capybara paws as fat, rounded pads with partial webbing — flattened spheres for the pad with small stubby, nubby toes tipped with dark nails, spread forward. I'm placing the sole near ground level with toe capsules slightly raised so the bottom sits at y=0.

Now moving to the hind legs: hip joints sit higher and further back, with a big haunch sphere for the thigh, then a bent three-segment limb running hip to knee to hock to foot to give that characteristic capybara crouch.

Legs under the belly only show as short stubs given current proportions, so I should raise the body and reduce its height to expose more leg length. Adjusting body center to y=0.40 with height 0.46 gives a bottom around 0.17, which better matches a realistic capybara shoulder height near 0.60 total.

Working out leg joint positions and segment lengths for both front and hind legs, with slight bends at the elbow and hip so they don't look perfectly straight. Sweeping the leg tubes with tapering radii for a smoother, more natural limb shape, then moving on to shaping the tail.

Since capybaras barely have a visible tail, I'm adding just a tiny nub stub with a small joint for rigging. For coloring, I'm planning a warm reddish-brown coat with lighter underparts and a darker muzzle, using countershading and fur mottling for texture, plus a gradient near the nose to darken it.

Writing custom paint logic... I'm also setting up scattered fur cards across the body—hundreds of small pointed tufts with varied size and lean angle to give that coarse, shaggy capybara-hair look.

For whimsical extras, I want to add a tiny chubby bird perched on the head—an egg-shaped body with a teal-blue back, cream-yellow belly, orange beak and feet, little red cheeks, and small tail/wing feathers to give it a cute, rounded character.

I'm planning the bird's rig: a birdBody joint parented to the capybara's head crown, with separate head, beak/jaw, two-joint wing chains, a two-joint tail, and simple legs, positioning it so the whole figure's total height comes out around 0.79 meters. I'm also thinking about extra storybook touches, like a tiny flower tucked behind the capybara's ear to complement the bird.

For the capybara's face, I'm settling on simple charm details: a daisy behind the ear, blush decals on the cheeks, whisker-dot freckles on the muzzle, and calm half-closed eyes rendered as dark ellipses with a brown lid arc to give that serene capybara look.

Shaping the lid geometry...

Adjusting the lid tilt so the gaze point sits right at the boundary gives a nice upper-half-lidded look, which I'll verify in preview. For the mouth, I'm thinking a thin dark draped line from the nose corner back toward the cheek with a slight upturn for a whimsical smile.

Adding whiskers next -- five per side radiating from the muzzle, thin dark bezier sweeps tapering outward, plus small fur tufts at the cheeks and smaller fur cards on the head. Then I'm moving on to the bird rig: setting up a body joint under the head, positioning its center just above the crown point by casting a ray down from the head surface, and figuring out which direction it should face.

I'm deciding to orient the bird slightly turned rather than facing straight forward, around 25-30 degrees, for a more playful look. I'm sketching a small coordinate helper that maps bird-local right/up/forward offsets into model space under this rotation, so I can build the bird's body parts and chains by calling this helper with simple local coordinates instead of hand-computing rotated positions each time.

I'm now sizing the body itself—roughly 0.13m long, egg-shaped with a scaled sphere or a short lofted sweep so it reads as chunky and round rather than flat, keeping that whimsical feel.

Then I'll layer the head as a slightly merged ball shape with countershaded coloring, add little crest feathers and blush cheeks for character, and build the beak as separate upper and lower cone wedges joined at a tiny jaw hinge.

For the wings, I'm thinking a two-joint chain per side, but rather than fully extending them I want a cute compromise pose—wings held slightly spread and raised like a balancing gesture, which feels more whimsical and readable than either tightly folded or fully outstretched.

Writing feather extrusion logic...

I'm planning the tail as a two-joint bone chain extending back from the body with three fanning feather extrudes colored dark blue with cream tips, and the legs as thin orange stick bones running from the body bottom toward the head crown area.

For legs, I'm keeping it minimal: a single-span bone chain from hip to foot, with rigid toe capsules attached to the foot bone (three forward, one back) rather than giving toes their own joints, keeping the overall triangle count low.

Now I'm picking the bird's palette — going for a cheerful bluebird look with a teal-blue back, darker wings, cream-yellow belly, orange beak, and red crest, since blue contrasts nicely against the brown capybara. For the capybara I'm settling on warm browns: a darker back, mottled shading, lighter flanks, and a pale belly tone.

I'm fleshing out capybara details — dark snout, black nose, pink-inside ears, orange-tinted incisors, dark whiskers, small cheek blush decals, and darker toes with pads. I'm also planning a little daisy accessory behind the ear with white petals and a yellow center, plus maybe a tiny leaf, and considering whether a fur tuft or mohawk detail would add more whimsy.

Now I'm setting up the color palette constraints and starting to write the actual builder code, being careful to use literal world coordinates for mirrored joints rather than relying on ambiguous local axes. Writing component setup code...

Still defining spine and neck chains...

I'm laying out seven loft stations from rump to shoulder with widths and heights tapering at each end, then figuring out how the rounded cap at the rump dome extends the silhouette slightly past the path's z=-0.52 endpoint.

I should rescale the whole body to a more compact, whimsical proportion—shrinking total length to roughly 1.25-1.3 m by moving the rump endpoint to around z=-0.45 to -0.50 and redistributing the intermediate stations accordingly.

Now I'm pinning down concrete joint coordinates: hips at [0,0.38,-0.24], spine running forward through a few points to the neck around z=0.32-0.44, and a head/jaw joint near [0,0.43,0.44] to [0,0.325,0.54], setting up the body loft stations from the rump forward with specific widths and heights at each.

Defining head loft stations...

Still adjusting snout taper dimensions...

I'm adding a nose cap using a flattened sphere to cover the front opening, bringing total head length to about 1.31 units, then moving on to construct the lower jaw stations starting from the jaw joint point.

Now I'm working out the jaw loft stations with their widths and heights, adjusting the final station position so the rounded cap stays within the nose boundary while letting the jaw top overlap slightly with the head bottom for a closed-mouth look. I'm deciding to paint the jaw with a tan shade for a slightly lighter chin.

Checking that the throat stays visible beneath the head given the body's height and bottom position confirms the jaw bottom placement works. Then I'm placing the eyes on the head surface at the appropriate height and offset, and positioning the ears near the head's top with an outward-and-upward orientation and a slightly elongated spherical shape.

I'm working out the exact facing direction and shape for the rounded capybara ears, flattened and angled sideways-back, with a smaller pink inner-ear sphere offset along that same direction. Now I'm shifting to positioning a bird perched on top of the capybara's head, figuring out where its crown should sit relative to the head's curve.

For skin detail, I'm setting up a raycast downward onto the head surface to find exact placement coordinates, then adding decals for blush and freckles — soft pink circular marks positioned on the cheeks, oriented outward from the head's surface normal.

Now I'm adding whisker-pad dot patterns on the muzzle sides, then working out the shoulder joint positions for the forelegs based on the body's dimensions, making sure the limb attachment points sit just inside the body's outer edge before defining the front limb geometry.

Writing leg sweep code...

Setting up the hind leg similarly with hip, knee, hock, and foot joints, naming each segment and deciding on a three-bone chain with knee bending forward and hock bending back.

I'm considering whether to add a chubby haunch sphere near the hip for a whimsical rounded look, but deciding to skip it for now and check the sweep radii for the legs before revisiting.

For the back, I'm planning three toes using a shared helper, skipping paw pads, and giving the tail a small two-joint chain ending in a stubby tapered sweep in a darker coat color rather than a single nub or cone. Then I'll move on to adding surface features to the body.

Scattering fur cards across the body's loft surface with varied size, lean, and bend, tinted to match the coat color but with slight variation using a fur tuft texture of layered grey gradient strands.

For the head, I'm placing smaller cards on the cheeks and adding an upward forehead crest, filtering by position so tufts cluster near the top. I'm also considering tiny brown eyebrow cones for expression, but thinking a neck/cheek ruff filter is getting too complex, so I'll simplify to general head-area scattering with a coarser filter instead.

Now I'm working out the whiskers as angled bezier curves fanning from the muzzle, four per side, thin dark strands with pointed caps. Then I'm placing a bean-shaped nose pad as a small ellipsoid on top of the snout, with two darker nostril ellipsoids positioned just below.

I'm also shaping the front muzzle pad as a rounded ellipsoid, adding a philtrum line down to the mouth, and positioning small cream teeth boxes just below the upper lip for a whimsical buck-toothed look.

Now I'm sweeping the mouth line along the head surface from the front dip up into a slight smile curve toward the cheek, using a thin dark stroke, then moving on to the coat coloring with a mottled countershading pattern between two body tones.

I'm shading the head coat darker toward the snout using a gradient blend, then applying the same head coat paint to the decorative cards, before shifting to work on the bird's local-to-world coordinate mapping.

I'm setting up a rotated origin point and yaw angle, then writing a helper function that converts bird-local coordinates into world space by applying the rotation transform.

Still defining the bird skeleton joints...

Now I'm sketching the body geometry: a scaled sphere for the torso with countershading paint (blue back, yellow belly), attached to the birdBody bone. The head is a smaller sphere positioned forward and up, slightly overlapping the body's top to keep proportions compact.

For coloring, I'm giving the head a blue top blending into cream cheeks using a countershade paint, then adding an orange-red crest made of three small feather spikes angled backward plus a tiny cowlick curl. Finally I'm placing dark eye spheres symmetrically near the front of the head.

Now I'm working out eye placement precisely on the head sphere surface, adding small white highlight dots, placing pink blush ellipsoids on the cheeks, and starting the beak as a cone-shaped spike running from a base point near the face down to its tip.

For the lower jaw I'm sizing a smaller spike bone and setting the cone sides to 6 for a faceted look. Now I'm shaping the wings, positioning shoulder, wrist, and tip points to angle outward and slightly up and back so they look like they're balancing, and planning the feather fan from there.

Defining feather outline shape...

For feather colors, I'm planning a gradient from a darker blue base to a lighter tip color, varying by position along the feather's length. For the wing structure, I'm sweeping capsule bones from shoulder to wrist to tip with tapering radii, then attaching feathers that radiate outward from the wing bones, distinguishing primaries and secondaries by which bone segment they're placed on.

Now I'm working out the tail: a chain of bone points stepping back and up, with five feathers fanning out horizontally in a spread of angles while pitched slightly upward, using a perpendicular direction derived from crossing the up vector with the feather's forward direction to get the horizontal spread axis. The tail feathers get their own size and dark blue with cream-tip coloring.

For the legs, since the body sits low and the feet should grip near the crown, I'm essentially hiding the legs and just showing small orange toe capsules emerging forward from the foot position, embedded into the head fur, with the body origin nudged down slightly below the crown surface so the toes sink in convincingly.

For the bird, I'll skip extra accessories like a scarf and just give it a simple crest tuft, leaving a flower for the capybara to hold instead. I'm placing a tiny daisy near the capybara's ear on the side facing the camera, roughly behind and slightly above it, so it reads well from a three-quarter front-left view.

Writing flower geometry code...

I'm also adding whimsical touches like tiny webbed toes with dark nails and belly fur details, thinking about density targets for the fur cards to keep the richness balanced against triangle count.

I'm planning the coat shading by layering a mottled base color with a darker countershaded belly and a dorsal stripe derived from surface normals, alongside smaller features like ear interiors, whiskers, teeth, eyebrow tufts, blush, and freckles. I'm building the paint function that composes these layers...

Blending mottle with fine grain streaks...

I'm thinking about texel density for a 1024 paint sheet across the model's surface area, keeping grain size around 0.02 for performance, plus setting up an SVG card texture at 128 size. I also want to make sure every part gets a name and a defined color, and I'm considering using a sweep for the loft geometry.

Now I'm working through the bone hierarchy for the loft — hips, spine, neck — and noticing a problem: the hips joint and the first spine joint sit at the same position, creating a zero-length bone that would cause weird projection artifacts. I'm adjusting the joint positions so hips has actual length before connecting into the spine chain, moving it slightly back so there's a real gap before the first spine joint.

I'm also sorting out parenting for the limbs: hind legs attach to hips, front legs attach to the last spine joint (spine3), and the neck chain parents off spine3 as well, with the head joint parenting off the neck chain. Everything lines up spatially, so now I'm setting side naming conventions (right/left to R/L) and starting to write out the ear geometry details.

Now I'm working out eye placement by finding the nearest surface point on the head loft, then seating the eye sphere along that surface normal with a slight embed offset so it sits naturally in the skull, and figuring out how to position the eyelid relative to the computed eye center.

I'll find the nearest point on the skull surface near that position and pull the eye center slightly inward along the normal, then place a small white highlight sphere offset outward from that point.

Deciding to keep eyebrows minimal since the sleepy lid already conveys the look, and sketching out the mouth drape next.

Setting the mouth drape path with a slight lift and catmull-rom knots, then checking that the loft for the head works correctly as a single rigid bone chain. I'm also settling on polygon detail levels—around 10 sides for the body and head, 8 for legs—to keep that whimsical low-poly but soft feel, then starting to sketch a helper function for building paw toes.

Writing leg chain code...

Finalizing the leg sweep radii, then checking the paw placement—making sure the rounded tube cap at the foot stays within acceptable floor tolerance, and sizing an ellipsoid paw shape at the correct foot coordinates.

Now I'm working out toe geometry: computing lateral offsets for four front toes, positioning each toe's base and tip, and sizing capsule radii so the toe bottoms clear the floor, plus adding small dark nail spikes at each tip.

Setting up the hind leg chain with hip, knee, hock, and foot joints, folded to match the shorter distance to the ground target, then placing three forward-facing toes on the hind paw.

Now adding an optional haunch sphere for extra body volume, plus belly, tail stub, and head details like orange-cream incisors, a dark nose pad with nostrils, and finding the skull's crown height via a raycast to position features relative to the head top.

Writing texture SVG...

Card colors get tinted multiplicatively with grey shading so fur darkens toward the root. I'm scattering hits across body and head surfaces with filters for position and normal direction, varying density and size between regions, and skipping chest/cheek ruff and feet details for now. Then I'm setting up a gradient paint for the head to darken toward the snout.

I'm applying a similar gradient to lighten the jaw, then designing a blush decal using soft overlapping ellipses in pink tones rather than relying on hard alpha cutoffs, and placing it as a decal on the skull with a defined position, direction, and size.

Now I'm sketching a feather helper function that computes perpendicular axes from a direction vector and extrudes an outline with specified thickness, bevel, and gradient coloring.

I'm figuring out the color blending using smoothstep between base and tip colors based on position along the feather, and planning the geometry for primary feathers on the wing—looping through angles and computing local directions rotated by the bird's orientation, anchored at the wrist position.

Working out secondaries, coverts, and tail feathers now—placing each set at different anchor points with varying lengths, widths, and angles to form a layered plumage effect, with coverts getting a lighter blue tint.

For the crest, I'm sketching three curved spike sweeps on the head using bezier paths, tilted outward at the sides and taller in the center, colored orange-red to give it that spiky crown look. I'll skip the eye ring detail and move on to writing the actual build code.

input.command: mkdir -p scratch/capybaraSonnet; grep -n "export" src/skeleton.ts | head -30; grep -n "export" src/ik.ts
